The cook before the chef

I learned to cook standing on a stool in my grandmother’s kitchen in the Beaujolais, shelling peas into a bowl and being trusted, at nine, with the tasting spoon. She cooked for whoever was in the house — family, pickers, a neighbour who had “just called in” at noon and left at four. Nobody wrote anything down. You tasted, you judged, you adjusted.

At twenty I took the other education: a Lyon bouchon, six years from commis to chef de partie. Service taught me speed and sauce discipline — quenelles by the hundred, a stockpot that never empties, a pass that never waits. It also taught me what I did not want: to cook all my life for people I would never see eat.

So since 2019 I cook in other people’s kitchens. I shop at Les Halles the morning of your dinner, I bring my own knives and one heavy pan, and I leave your kitchen cleaner than I found it. Four hundred and eighty dinners in, the rule from my grandmother’s kitchen still runs the pass: taste before you judge — then serve.

A market morning, in four stops

Her milestones, on market time
  1. 05.40Her grandmother’s kitchen

    Sundays in a farmhouse kitchen in the Beaujolais: one wood stove, nine cousins, and the rule that you taste before you judge.

  2. 06.10The bistro years

    Commis, then chef de partie, in a Lyon bouchon — six years of service speed, sauce discipline and quenelles by the hundred.

  3. 07.00The first private client

    A neighbour’s sixtieth in Croix-Rousse, cooked on two burners and one borrowed oven. She never went back to a restaurant kitchen.

  4. 08.20Four hundred and eighty dinners

    The practice today: one chef, one market run each morning, a second cookbook out — and a waiting list for Saturdays.

Before you ask

Can you cook for allergies and dietary requirements?

Yes — and the menu is rebuilt around them, not patched. Coeliac, vegetarian, a grandfather who cannot manage rich food: tell her when you book and it is simply how the menu is written. Late surprises have been handled too, but early is kinder.

How far ahead should we book?

Weekends go three to four months out — Saturdays first. Weekday lunches are sometimes possible inside a month. A 30% deposit holds your date; nothing is promised to anyone else in the meantime.

Our kitchen is small. Is that a problem?

One oven and two burners is enough — it describes most of the kitchens she cooks in. She brings her own knives, one heavy pan and a cool box. The wedding breakfast for twenty-two was cooked in a studio kitchen in Fourvière.

Who serves, and who washes up?

Camille cooks and plates; above ten guests she brings a server she trusts. And the kitchen is left cleaner than she found it — it is written into her proposal, half as a joke and entirely in earnest.

How does booking work?

A short call, then a written menu proposal within three days. The deposit holds the date, the balance is due on the night. No surprises: the calculator on this page is the real rate card.
